title: Value iteration
objectives: Code value iteration and bound its error by the discount factor.

screens.title: One look ahead
screens.prose: On the deterministic grid, suppose every cell's value is 0 to begin with. At row 1, column 4 the agent can try each move and score it by reward plus $0.9 \times$ the value of the cell it lands in.
screens.question: What is the best score among the four moves at row 1, column 4? Give a decimal to 2 places.

hints.text: R enters the +1 cell, which ends the episode.
That move pays $1 - 0.04$, and the end cell is worth 0.
Every other move pays −0.04 and lands on a 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Score each move by reward plus 0.9 times the landing value.

byKey.no-step: You left out the step cost of the move into the +1.
byKey.disc: The +1 is paid on this move, so it is not discounted.
byKey.bump: That is the score of a move that does not reach the +1.

explain.text: Moving R pays 0.96 at once; every other move pays −0.04. Taking the best score as the cell's new value is one **backup**. Do it for every cell and repeat.

screens.title: Values spread from the goal
screens.prose: Each sweep backs up every cell once, using the previous sweep's values. Slide through the sweeps on the deterministic grid. The arrows show the best move under the current values.
screens.question: On which sweep does the start cell, row 4 column 1, first get a positive value?

hints.text: A sweep lets news travel one cell further from the goal.
The start is seven moves from the +1.
Before the news arrives, the start only sees step costs.

feedback.correct: Sweep 7: the start is seven moves from the goal.
feedback.generic: Slide until the start cell turns positive.

byKey.six: After sweep 6 the start is still at −0.1874: the goal is seven moves away.
byKey.eight: Sweep 8 changes nothing: the values had already settled.
byKey.one: After sweep 1 only the cells next to the end cells have heard about them.

explain.text: Sweep $k$ gives each cell the best return over $k$ moves. The start, seven moves away, turns positive on sweep 7, at 0.3228, and sweep 8 changes nothing. Before that it shows only the step costs, −0.04, −0.076 and so on.

screens.title: Value iteration
screens.prose: Repeating the backup $$V(s) \leftarrow \max_a \sum_{s'} p(s' \mid s, a)\,[\,r + \gamma V(s')\,]$$ for every cell is **value iteration**. On the slippery grid the intended move succeeds with 0.8 and each side slip has 0.1. Start again from all zeros.
screens.question: After the first sweep on the slippery grid, what is the value at row 1, column 4? Give a decimal to 2 places.

hints.text: R reaches the +1 with 0.8; a slip U bumps the edge; a slip D reaches row 2.
The two slips each pay −0.04 and land on a 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average over the three outcomes of moving R.

byKey.det: That is the deterministic value. Here R succeeds only 8 times in 10.
byKey.no-slip-cost: You left out the step cost on the two slips.
byKey.slip-pit: A slip from row 1 cannot reach the pit: down from column 4 is row 2, column 4.

explain.text: Moving R: $0.8 \times 0.96 + 0.2 \times (-0.04) = 0.76$. No other move does better. Later sweeps raise it to 0.8896 as the cells around it gain value.

screens.title: Why walk away from the goal?
screens.prose: Value iteration on the slippery grid settles on the values shown. Next to the pit, at row 3 column 5, the best move is L, away from the goal.
screens.question: Using the values shown, what is the score of moving U at row 3, column 5? Give a decimal to 4 places.

hints.text: U enters the pit with 0.8.
A slip L reaches row 3 column 4; a slip R hits the edge and stays.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average the three outcomes of moving U.

byKey.no-slip: You took U as certain. It slips sideways two times in ten.
byKey.l: That is the score of L, the best move. The question asks about U.
byKey.sign: Check the sign: falling in the pit 8 times in 10 makes this move's score negative.
byKey.pit-later: The pit pays $-1 - 0.04$ on entry and then ends: no discount on it.

explain.text: U scores -0.7896 because it falls in the pit 8 times in 10. L scores 0.1634: it heads round by row 3, column 4, and risks the pit only on a 0.1 slip. Slips change the best route, not just the values.

screens.title: How fast it settles
screens.prose: Each backup is a **contraction**: it shrinks the largest gap between any two value tables by at least $\gamma$. So after $k$ sweeps the error is at most $\gamma^k$ times the first. The chart shows the largest change made by each slippery sweep, on a log scale, beside that bound.
screens.question: On the slippery grid, on which sweep does the largest change first fall below $10^{-6}$?

hints.text: Follow the slippery curve down to the dashed line.
It crosses between sweeps 24 and 25.
Sweep 24 changes by $1.34 \times 10^{-6}$; sweep 25 by $6.2 \times 10^{-7}$.

feedback.correct: Sweep 25 is the first to change by less than $10^{-6}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read where the slippery curve crosses $10^{-6}$.

byKey.det: The deterministic grid settles after 8 sweeps. Slips make values depend on loops, which take longer.
byKey.bound: That is the guarantee from $0.9^k \le 10^{-6}$, which needs 132 sweeps. The real changes fall faster than the bound.

explain.text: The slippery changes fall by about half a sweep at the end, faster than the guaranteed 0.9, and drop below $10^{-6}$ on sweep 25 (38 to $10^{-10}$). The deterministic changes follow $0.96 \times 0.9^{k-1}$ exactly, then stop at sweep 8. The bound $\gamma^k$ never fails, but it can be loose.

screens.title: The dice game, one state
screens.prose: The unlimited dice game from l5 is value iteration with a single state: repeat $V \leftarrow E[\max(X, 0.9V)]$ from $V = 0$. The first sweep gives 3.5.
screens.question: What does the second sweep give? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: Keep 4, 5 or 6; replace 1, 2 and 3 by 3.15.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the larger of each roll and 3.15, then average.

byKey.undisc: That is the two-roll game with no discount. Here a reroll is worth $0.9 \times 3.5$.
byKey.mean: That is the first sweep again.
byKey.keep-all: You averaged the six rolls and 3.15 as seven numbers.

explain.text: $E[\max(X, 3.15)] = (15 + 3 \times 3.15)/6 = 4.075$. Further sweeps give 4.334, 4.450, 4.503, and close in on 4.5833 by at least a factor 0.9 each time.

screens.title: Updating in place
screens.prose: A colleague's value iteration writes each new value into the table straight away, so later cells in the same sweep use it. You expected every cell to use the previous sweep's table.
screens.question: What should you tell the colleague?

options.text: It is fine: in-place sweeps reach the same values, here in fewer sweeps
It is a bug: mixing old and new values gives wrong answers
options.why: Each in-place update is still a backup towards the same fixed point. It converges to the same values, often faster.

options.text: It works, but always needs more sweeps
options.why: Here it needed 17 sweeps against 25: new values pass on within the sweep.

options.text: It only works if the cells are swept from the goal outwards
options.why: Any order converges. Sweeping from the goal can be faster still, but it is not needed.

hints.text: Is an in-place update still a backup?
Every backup moves the table towards the same fixed point.
Compare the sweep counts in the table.

feedback.correct: In-place sweeps (Gauss-Seidel) converge to the same values.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask whether the fixed point changes.

byKey.bug: You took mixing old and new values for an error. The fixed point is the same, so the answer is the same.

explain.text: Using fresh values within a sweep is Gauss-Seidel value iteration: same fixed point, here 17 sweeps instead of 25. The other trap is stopping when the arrows stop changing and quoting those values as exact: the policy settles before the values do.

screens.title: Code value iteration
screens.prose: Write `value_iteration(slip, gamma, tol)`: sweep from zeros, each new table built from the previous one, and stop after the first sweep whose largest change is below `tol`. Return the values and the number of sweeps. Then `greedy_policy`, returning for each cell every action within $10^{-9}$ of the best.
screens.question: Complete `value_iteration` and `greedy_policy`.

widget.how: Submit runs 11 hidden tests. Sweep counts and action sets must equal ours; values must match within 1e-6.

mutants.symptom: Writes each new value straight into V: 17 sweeps, not 25.
End cells are not held at 0.
greedy_policy keeps one best action, dropping ties.
Ties by q == best; passes because tied floats happen to be equal here.

hints.text: Build the whole new table before replacing the old one.
End cells stay at 0.
Compare with `best - 1e-9` so ties keep every best action.

feedback.correct: All pass. On the deterministic grid seven cells have two best actions.
feedback.generic: Some tests fail. Check that each sweep reads only the previous table, and that you count the final sweep.

explain.text: A synchronous sweep needs a fresh table each time; the count includes the sweep that drops below `tol`. Returning a set per cell keeps tied actions, which lesson 8 needs to compare policies fairly.

screens.title: More than one best move
screens.prose: On the deterministic grid the start, row 4 column 1, is seven moves from the goal by several routes.
screens.question: Select all the moves that are optimal at the start. Select all that apply.

options.why: Down runs off the grid: the agent stays and wastes a step.
Left runs off the grid: a wasted step.

hints.text: Compare the cells the moves lead to.
U reaches row 3 column 1, R reaches row 4 column 2.
Both show 0.4031.

feedback.correct: U and R both lead to a cell worth 0.4031, so both score $-0.04 + 0.9 \times 0.4031 = 0.3228$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Score each move from the values shown.

explain.text: U and R tie exactly. Any policy that picks either is optimal, so "the optimal policy" is really a set of actions per cell. Comparing two policies by one arg-max would report a false difference here.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: Value iteration repeats $$V_{k+1}(s) = \max_a \sum_{s'} p(s' \mid s, a)[r + \gamma V_k(s')].$$ For $\gamma < 1$ each sweep is a contraction, so $\max_s |V_k(s) - V^*(s)| \le \gamma^k \max_s |V_0(s) - V^*(s)|$. The greedy actions of $V^*$ form the optimal policy, ties included.
screens.question: Starting 1.0 from $V^*$ at most, with $\gamma = 0.9$, what does the bound promise after 50 sweeps?

options.why: The bound shrinks but is never 0 in finitely many sweeps; the deterministic grid happens to settle exactly.

options.text: An error of at most $1 - 50 \times 0.1$, which is negative
options.why: The error shrinks by a factor each sweep, not by a fixed amount.
That would be one halving. Fifty sweeps at 0.9 shrink it by $0.9^{50}$.

feedback.generic: Raise 0.9 to the number of sweeps.

screens.title: An American put, one node
screens.prose: On a binomial tree, an American put with strike £100 sits at a node where the stock is £92. One step on, the put is worth £4.10 if the stock rises and £11.80 if it falls, each with risk-neutral chance 0.5. One step's discount factor is 0.99.
screens.question: What is the put worth at this node, in pounds?

hints.text: There are two actions: exercise now, or hold.
Exercising pays $100 - 92$. Holding is worth $0.99 \times$ the average next value.
Take the larger of 8 and $0.99 \times 7.95$.

feedback.correct: Exercise pays £8; holding is worth $0.99 \times 7.95 = 7.8705$. The put is worth £8: exercise.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare exercising now with holding one more step.

byKey.cont: That is the value of holding. Exercising now pays £8, which is more.
byKey.undisc: You left out the discount, and exercising still pays more.
byKey.down: That is the value after a fall only.

explain.text: The backup is $\max(\text{exercise}, \text{hold}) = \max(8, 0.99 \times 7.95) = 8$. Pricing an American option is this backup run from the last step back, with "exercise" as an action, as `graphs-dp` did for the dice game.

ideas: Value iteration repeats the optimal backup $V(s) \leftarrow \max_a \sum_{s'} p\,[r + \gamma V(s')]$ for every state, from any start, until the change is small.

Each sweep is a contraction: for $\gamma < 1$ the error shrinks by at least $\gamma$, so $k$ sweeps leave at most $\gamma^k$ of it. Real changes can fall faster: 25 sweeps to $10^{-6}$ on the slippery grid.
The greedy actions of the final values are optimal, and ties are common: an optimal policy is a set of actions per state.

formula.name: Bellman optimality backup
formula.note: Converges to $V^*$ from any start when $\gamma < 1$.

summary.trap: Calling an in-place update a bug (it converges too), or stopping when the arrows stop changing and quoting those values as exact.

quiz.prose: Deterministic grid. A cell's four moves lead to cells worth 0.5914, 0.4923, 0.4923 and itself (a bump, worth 0.30 now).
quiz.question: What is its value after one backup? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Score the best move: $-0.04 + 0.9 \times$ its landing value.

byKey.no-step: You left out the step cost.

explain.text: The best move leads to 0.5914, so the backup gives $-0.04 + 0.9 \times 0.5914 = 0.4923$.

quiz.prose: Value iteration with $\gamma = 0.5$ starts at most 2.0 from $V^*$.
quiz.question: How many sweeps guarantee an error below 0.001?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the smallest $k$ with $2 \times 0.5^k < 0.001$.

byKey.ten: At 10 sweeps the bound is 0.00195, still above 0.001.
byKey.log: You counted decimal places. Each sweep only halves the error.

quiz.prose: After a few sweeps of value iteration the greedy arrows stop changing.
quiz.question: What can you say about the values at that point?

options.text: They may still be some way from $V^*$, even though the policy is already optimal
They equal $V^*$, because the policy is optimal
options.why: The policy often settles first; the values keep moving until the change is tiny.

options.text: The policy must be wrong, since the values are still changing
options.why: A policy can be optimal while the values are still converging.

options.text: The run can stop and report those values as exact
options.why: That is the trap: report values only once the change per sweep is below your tolerance.

feedback.correct: The arrows settle before the numbers.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Do the values have to have converged for the arrows to be right?

explain.text: Greedy actions depend only on which move scores best, so they settle early. The values converge only at the rate $\gamma$; quote them once the change is small.
